analysis.one_liner: Bars lawsuits against food companies claiming their products caused obesity or weight gain.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee after a single subcommittee hearing until the Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it illegal to sue food manufacturers, sellers, advertisers, and their trade associations in any federal or state court for claims that their products caused weight gain, obesity, or related health problems. It would also have thrown out any such lawsuits already in progress. It kept narrow exceptions: suits over food that was adulterated, suits where a company knowingly broke a law about making or selling the food, and contract or warranty claims. The bill never left the Senate Judiciary Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Food and restaurant companies, advertisers, distributors, and their trade associations. They would be shielded from court claims that their marketing or products contributed to obesity, including suits over how food is marketed to children. The shield would apply retroactively to pending cases.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Food and restaurant companies and advertisers

how_it_helps.text: The bill forbids any 'qualified civil liability action' — a lawsuit over injuries from weight gain or obesity — from being brought in any federal or state court against food manufacturers, marketers, distributors, advertisers, sellers, or trade associations [S2][S3].
Any such lawsuit already pending when the bill took effect would have been dismissed immediately by the court hearing it [S2][S3].
The ban would have covered suits for money damages and for injunctions — court orders telling a company to change its conduct, such as how it markets food [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers who suffer obesity-related health problems and believe a company's products or marketing contributed would lose their day in court, with no substitute remedy created. Courts and state governments would also lose the power to hear these claims or seek injunctions against food marketing practices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers seeking to sue over obesity-related harm

drawbacks.text: The shield is broad: it covers not just manufacturers but also marketers, advertisers, and trade associations, and it wipes out pending lawsuits, eliminating any court check on how food is marketed for weight-related harm [S3].

Supporters would argue the exceptions are meaningful — the bill still allows suits where a company knowingly and willfully violated a statute governing the food's manufacture, marketing, or labeling, and suits over adulterated food [S3]. An honest supporter would also note the cost: food companies face open-ended liability for personal dietary choices, which could mean higher prices and defensive business practices across the food industry.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit — freeing a lawful industry from a wave of speculative lawsuits over personal eating choices — comes entirely at the expense of consumers' access to the courts. The narrow carve-outs for knowingly illegal conduct and adulterated food are sensible, but the core of the bill is a one-way transfer of legal protection to the food industry without any offsetting protection for the public. Its death meant the trade-off was never accepted.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which held one subcommittee hearing but never voted it out, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Sen. Mitch McConnell introduced the bill on July 17, 2003, with 19 cosponsors (15 Republicans and 4 Democrats) [S1][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary on the day of introduction [S5].
The Judiciary Subcommittee on Administrative Oversight and the Courts held a hearing on October 16, 2003 — the bill's only action beyond referral [S5].
The full Judiciary Committee never reported the bill, and neither the Senate nor the House ever voted on it; it died at the end of the 108th Congress on January 3, 2005 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary consumers kept the ability to take obesity-related claims to court, and the food and restaurant industries did not get the lawsuit shield they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers who kept their right to sue

for.name: Food and restaurant industry
for.role: National trade groups representing restaurants and food manufacturers
for.what_they_did: Backed legislation shielding food companies from obesity lawsuits, which they saw as a threat to their business.

against.what_they_did: Opposed limits on lawsuits against the food industry, which would eliminate a category of contingency-fee cases.

sides.party_line_note: The cosponsor list leaned heavily Republican (15 of 19), with only 4 of the Senate's 48 Democrats signing on, and the bill died quietly in a Republican-run committee without a floor vote [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have given them near-total immunity from suits claiming their food or marketing caused obesity, including suits over marketing to children. Their gain would have come directly at the cost of consumers' legal remedies. The bill died, so no immunity was granted.

They would be shielded from obesity-related claims in any state or federal court, with pending suits dismissed. The carve-outs for adulterated food and knowing violations of law would have left narrow exposure. The bill died, so the shield never took effect.

The bill's coverage of 'marketers' and 'advertisers' would have protected companies that promote food products from injunctions or damages tied to weight-related harm. The bill died, so this protection never became law.

The bill would have eliminated an emerging category of consumer-injury lawsuits. In this case the industry-aligned loser's interest ran alongside consumers' interest in keeping access to the courts. The bill's death preserved those potential claims.
